text:
Crazy 72 hours in security. Three major incidents dropped back-to-back: eMudhra, PingCAP (TiDB Cloud), and PHP.

Here is the short version of what happened and who got hit.

1. eMudhra (Trusted CA compromise)

eMudhra generated 8 intermediate CA certificates in April 2025 (cross-signed by Sectigo). A bug in their HSM key-wrapping test script created a second set of P-384 keys where the private keys were single-byte numbers under 256. Operators picked the wrong key labels and signed them into real CA certs.

One of the intermediate CA private keys was literally the number 4.
The other seven: 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237.

Three weeks later (May 2025), their CRL signatures started failing because the CRL signer was using the real keys instead of the weak ones. Instead of asking why the keys didn't match, someone switched the CRL signer to the weak keys and closed the ticket.

• Browsers are safe: Chrome, Firefox, Apple, and Microsoft already blocked them, and zero rogue certs hit CT logs.
• Servers are not: curl, Python (certifi), Go binaries, and Docker base images don't check CRLs. Update ca-certificates, certifi, and Go (1.27.3 / 1.26.10).
• 10-second check on any server:
  curl https://t.co/vhiGLxNhIS
  (TLS error = safe. 200 OK = still vulnerable.)

2. PingCAP / TiDB Cloud (10.6 TB breach)

Attackers found GCP and Azure credentials committed inside PingCAP's own repos. They set up a replication feed of TiDB Cloud's production control plane and exported the entire database every 6 hours for 22 straight days. 88 full exports, zero alerts. 200 GB is already out on torrents.

Beyond the 413 private repos and 20.6M customer SQL queries logged from their web SQL Editor, PingCAP engineers were pasting customer secrets into Jira tickets.

Who is affected in the leaked records:

• Live credentials exposed in support tickets:
  - Pinterest: AWS keys for their pingcap-logs S3 bucket
  - CardX / Silverlake (NPCI-linked env): AWS admin key in a backup log with full access to 258 external S3 buckets
  - DeBank: 38 presigned S3 URLs
  - An unnamed AI/dev platform: a 314 MB slow-query log attached to a ticket containing 8,027 live customer secrets (an AWS root key, a GitHub admin PAT over 1,701 repos, 7,485 AWS STS tokens, and 192 OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini keys)

• Tenants with infra metadata, VPC CIDRs, app-server IPs, or contract pricing exposed:
  - Tech: Atlassian, Databricks, Airbnb, Baidu, LINE, Nylas, Persona, PatSnap
  - E-comm & Travel: https://t.co/C512KFOEq5, Shopee, Flipkart, Mercari, ZOZO, AEON, Delhivery, Klook
  - Gaming: Capcom, Square Enix, Konami, Bandai Namco, Cygames, Colopl, DMM
  - Finance: PayPay, SoftBank, SBI, SB Payment Service, Fujitsu, TOPPAN, Bank of China, China Life
  - Crypto: Bitget (said only public trade logs were on it and they already left), Pionex, DigiPlus, NFTscan, Chainbase

• Developer profiles leaked (from a purchased https://t.co/28tjHqd5Wr table in PingCAP's BigQuery):
  - 24,900 personal emails + GitHub/LinkedIn profiles of engineers at Tencent (3,327), Huawei (2,726), ByteDance (2,475), AIG (2,140), Mastercard, Flipkart, and bKash.

If you use TiDB Cloud: rotate your console API keys, DB passwords, and anything you ever pasted into a support ticket.

3. PHP "PHP2Shell" (CVE-2026-109618 & CVE-2026-109619)

Two CVSS 9.2 pre-auth RCEs leaked yesterday ahead of today's 14:00 UTC patch.

Public writeups trace it to a heap Use-After-Free in PHP's native C multipart/form-data session upload-progress handler (ext/session/session.c).

Because C-level multipart parsing runs before line 1 of index.php:
• App auth, Laravel/WordPress middleware, and file_uploads = Off do not stop it.
• Only PHP 8.2–8.5 get official patches today (59% of PHP servers on Shodan are on EOL <= 8.1).
• Until you patch php-fpm: lock php_admin_flag[session.upload_progress.enabled] = off and block unexpected multipart requests at Nginx/Apache/Cloudflare.

text:
重大安全警告！互联网8把“万能钥匙”被破解，银行、交易所、Google都可能遭到冒充，请立即更新浏览器！

卧槽，这次互联网安全事故真的有点离谱！

印度数字证书机构 eMudhra 的8把CA私钥被发现存在致命缺陷，本该拥有384位安全强度的私钥，实际竟然只是4、56、66、115、155、156、230、237这8个数字。

安全研究员 Scott Helme 用普通笔记本不到1秒就恢复了全部私钥，而且这些证书从2025年4月就已经存在。

这事有多严重？

CA相当于互联网的身份认证机构，负责证明你访问的银行、Google、交易所究竟是不是真的。

攻击者掌握这些私钥，就有能力伪造任意网站的HTTPS证书，在仍然信任这些证书的设备上，配合网络流量劫持实施中间人攻击，窃取密码、API密钥，甚至篡改通信内容。

尤其是Crypto用户，交易机器人、交易所API和自动化钱包后端，都可能成为攻击目标。

目前 Google Chrome、Firefox已经紧急封锁涉事证书，Apple和Microsoft也采取了措施。

Chrome和Firefox的正常配置甚至不需要手动升级就能接收封锁更新，目前也没有证据表明发生了大规模恶意利用。

但Python、Node.js、Go、服务器、Docker容器及部分老旧设备，可能仍然信任这些证书，整个软件生态的清理远比浏览器复杂。

⚠️ 建议大家今天就做几件事：

更新Chrome、Firefox等浏览器及电脑、手机系统。

检查交易机器人、开发工具和服务器依赖是否有安全更新。

未完成更新前，尽量避免通过不可信网络执行敏感操作。

所有补丁只从官方渠道安装，任何所谓的证书修复工具或邮件都不要轻信。

text:
Regarding the PHP vulnerability, I have seen some security researchers recommending people limit web browsing for a few days (due to the potential for common websites to be compromised via this vuln).

There is exploit code available for this vuln, though it is not known to exist “in the wild.” But with the weaponization of AI, it’s possible that the discovery and broad distribution of exploit code could happen fast - possibly reverse engineered after the patches are released.

I expect cyber security providers of web application firewalls and exploit prevention services will have protections deployed quickly today, and IT teams will be busy patching and upgrading.

And I think it may be wise to lay low on the Internet today. Do what you need to, but probably skip frivolous browsing.

Also: 

Make sure you are running full service anti-virus / anti-malware on every device (including phones). I recommend BitDefender for home/personal use.

Update your browser apps and only use Safari, FireFox, or DuckDuckGo. No opinion about Brave (people keep asking). Make sure ad blocking is turned on and auto play of active content is turned off.

Be very cautious of links you receive in SMS messages, message apps, and email. Check and verify the source first and check the URL to make sure the website domain is as expected.

Keep your operating system and all applications up to date, and watch for new updates over the coming days. Regarding iOS, I do not recommend upgrading to 27. Stay on 26 and update as possible.

Make sure you have MFA turned on for all websites or online accounts. True MFA. Passkey has a major design weakness so I do not recommend it.

This is all to protect your devices and your accounts in case a website you visit is explored and does attempt to steal your credentials, information, or deliver exploit code to your device.

@PractiveSec will be following this today. Advisory coming for customers.

因为很多日本传统企业的IT support、devops是真不上网看圈外新闻，不看英文新闻和社区，也完全不管安全，任何新闻完完全全不关心。

如果高市早苗不提一句，他们能一直装傻充愣到几个月以后被真正攻击一次。

这种企业放在20年前，就应该老老实实用微软和oracle的技术，有问题直接推送更新， 服务商和外包直接线下一封封邮件发过去，甚至直接人工一个个打电话、发传真过去，告诉他们事情的紧急性，安排他们两周内开个会，帮他们手把手上门升级。

对于这些日本传统企业而言，这才是最安全、最正确、最及时的处理方式。

text:
一个日本女人，瞒着丈夫拍了整整两年AV。

直到她亲口坦白，丈夫才知道，自己每天生活在一起的妻子，竟然早已成了AV演员。

丈夫受到的打击有多大？

整整一个星期，他几乎都处于失魂落魄的状态，连觉都睡不好。

可更让人意外的是，这段婚姻不仅没有因此结束，夫妻关系反而比以前更好了。

2026年8月，日本40岁AV演员木下凛凛子，在接受《日刊SPA!》采访时，讲述了这段经历。

事情要从2020年说起。

那一年，她34岁，已经结婚。

随着年龄增长，她越来越在意自己的容貌，想趁着还年轻，留下当时的模样。

起初，她考虑过拍摄写真，也尝试寻找其他模特工作机会。

几次碰壁后，她产生了一个大胆的念头：

干脆去拍一部AV。

她原本只打算拍一部，留个纪念就退出。

没想到，真正进入这个行业后，她却继续做了下去。

而丈夫从头到尾都不知道。

最初，她以为自己可以一直隐瞒。

但随着工作越来越多，内心的愧疚也越来越重。

偏偏那段时间，她和丈夫的感情本来就不好。

两个人越来越少交流，夫妻关系逐渐冷淡。

她觉得丈夫不够重视自己，却又因为隐瞒了这么大的秘密，无法坦然面对他。

就这样过了两年。

终于有一天，她决定不再隐瞒。

她向丈夫表明，自己想按照喜欢的方式生活。

随后，坦白了自己的真实职业。

丈夫听完，受到了巨大冲击。

木下后来回忆，那一个星期，丈夫几乎一直处于失神状态，似乎连觉都睡不好。

但有件事出乎她的意料。

丈夫没有要求她退出AV行业。

他没有马上理解这一切，却也没有因此结束婚姻。

日子一天天过去。

丈夫渐渐发现，妻子虽然从事着一份自己难以接受的工作，但依然认真对待家庭，也非常投入自己的事业。

他的态度开始改变。

从最初的震惊、难以接受，到后来逐渐理解。

甚至当妻子出差工作时，他还会主动关心她的情况。

而原本已经越来越冷淡的夫妻关系，竟然慢慢回暖了。

2026年，40岁的木下凛凛子回头看这段经历，甚至感慨：

如果当初没有进入AV行业，她和丈夫的关系可能早就彻底冷掉了。

不过，这终究是木下本人讲述的经历，我们并不知道丈夫心里究竟经历了怎样的挣扎。

一个女人有权选择自己的职业。

一个丈夫也有权决定，自己能不能接受这样的婚姻。

但这件事真正让人纠结的，或许还不只是职业本身。

而是妻子整整两年的隐瞒。

text:
炒股软件居然也搞开源了，这操作属实有点离谱。

OpenStock 在 GitHub 上 star 已经 16900+，一个开源项目，把付费行情软件里那些要收你钱的功能，全给塞进一个免费平台，还放话永久免费。

它想干的事特别直接：一分钱不掏，也能用上一整套看盘工具。我拆开给你说：

1️⃣ 实时股价，行情随时盯着

2️⃣ TradingView 的 K 线，专业软件同款

3️⃣ 技术指标，该有的都有

4️⃣ Reddit、X、财经新闻、Polymarket 的市场情绪，全揉进一个界面，省得你开一堆网页来回切

最让我买账的是 Watchlist 这块。把持仓加进去，Gemini 会顺着你关注的方向，每天生成一份 AI 新闻摘要，直接推到你邮箱。

说白了，盯盘、看新闻、刷情绪、整理信息流这些事，它基本都给你捏一块儿了，一个界面搞定。

技术栈也不含糊，Next.js、TypeScript、MongoDB，还挂着 GitHub Trending 当日第一的牌子，不是那种随手写完就扔的玩具。

不过我得提一句，它自己也讲了，OpenStock 是社区搭起来的，不是券商，行情数据可能有延迟，里面的东西也不构成任何投资建议，你自己心里有数就行。

想上手的自己去扒源码：

🔗 https://t.co/z836jbyUdO

text:
有一次，孙哥携带我，和朋友们一起就餐。
在大家纷纷起身，觥筹交错，举杯畅饮之际。
他的敌蜜假装不经意地问：“孙哥，你多高。”
想要一举击溃孙哥。

没想到，孙哥居然面不改色地回答：“我1米75。”
我不可置信地看着他，那一瞬间，第一次体会到了来自爱人的背刺。

我以为爱情是两个人共同面对世界，没想到关键时刻，他竟然选择了独自长高。

“那你呢”客户问。
我看了看眼神坚毅的孙哥，为了爱情，我只好说，“我1米66。”

爱情的忠贞就在于此，
像险峰，增加你的高度，衬托你的威仪。
不仅爱你伟岸的身躯， 也爱你坚持的位置，足下的鞋垫。

text:
席卷全球！仅今天晚上，多个国家领导人、政府网络安全部门、AI 公司，纷纷就 PHP 编程语言重大漏洞紧急发文，包括芬兰、荷兰和法国在内，已将政府网站紧急下线。

而原因是今天 PHP，爆出两个超高危漏洞，合称 PHP2Shell，还是研究员借助 AI 发现的。黑客不用登录，发一个请求就可能控制整台网站服务器。

他们能通过这个漏洞，在你家用 PHP 搞的网站上，装木马、偷数据，甚至能把网站搞瘫。

据估算，暴露在互联网上的 PHP 服务器，已超 510 万台。

所以现在的情况是，PHP 团队紧急更新了补丁，要求所有人立刻马上升级。

而 CDN 厂商 Cloudflare 的 CTO 也说，已经看到有早期攻击现象出现。

英国国家网络安全中心 NCSC 也建议，补不了的系统先下线，欧洲有不少网站因此停掉。

Tibo 当场 @ 了 Sam Altman！！！就为了问一句自己是不是要凉了！！！

text:
#instabox.sh 很多人都不知道这玩意领了可以干什么？！

我来提供一下我自己的使用案例

先说它是什么：一台海外云电脑，Debian，自带 docker、chromium、claude、codex、node、python。免费层长期给 1 台 4 核 8G，不限用量。

我自己的用法：把它当成 24 小时的信息管家

1）RSSHub 自建
用 docker 一行命令起一个 RSSHub。没有 RSS 的网站，比如论坛热帖、留学版、OpenWrt 论坛，都能变成 RSS。自己搭的不用抢公共实例，也不会动不动被限流。

2）Miniflux 统一订阅
官方博客、GitHub releases、Reddit、羊毛区、RSSHub 生成的源，全都丢进 Miniflux（配 PostgreSQL）。设好自动清理：已读 7 天、未读 14 天归档，每周 清理一次，保障有效空间。

3）AI 先筛一遍
新文章先用便宜的分类模型打分，只有拿不准的才交给大模型复核。我给 500 条做了一次体检，粗筛只花了 2 美分。顺便按数据给每个源打分，一口气退订了 6 个水源。

4）翻译 + 早报 + 推到 Telegram
英文文章自动翻译，每天生成一份早报，用 RSStT 推到 Telegram。早上起来，整理好的中文信息流已经在手机上了。

5）再往下接
同一份 RSS 还能喂给别的流程：HN 和 HF Daily Papers 的热论文自动写导读；官方博客一有更新就提醒；内容选题直接从 RSS 里挑。

其他可以干的
- 跑 Claude Code / Codex：这台机器当 agent 的工作台，不占自己的电脑
- Cloudflare Tunnel：不用开端口，把里面的服务挂到自己的域名上
- GitHub webhook：仓库有人提 issue 或 PR，就叫醒机器自动审代码、写补丁，等我点头再推
- 自带 chromium：网页截图、录动画、跑爬虫
- 临时的文件下载站、小网站、Telegram 机器人

上边这些算是之前玩RSS的人传统艺能了！

目前绝大多数 API 的 Prompt Cache，生命周期基本卡在 12 小时以内。超过这个窗口，缓存自动失效，状态全部清空

但 Codex 和 Work 的做法直接跳出了纯 API 的逻辑：把缓存与登录用户深度绑定，做到跨会话、跨周期的永久保留

哪怕一个重型项目你放置了几天甚至几周，只要重新拉起旧对话，上下文依然能稳定命中

这东西最大的价值不在于省了多少毫秒的延迟，而在于重构了 Agent 的经济模型：

边际成本被直接按死：缓存命中的 Token 价格直接下探到正常输入的 1/20（降幅 95%）。

1. 长任务的冷启动成本归零：在几十万 Token 的工程级代码库里，反复交互最烧钱的从来不是新生成的内容，而是每次回车都必须重新过一遍全部历史上下文。

2. 订阅制 Agent 的生产力杠杆放大：同样的月度配额，以前跑几个长周期任务额度就见底，现在等同于把有效交互轮次拉高了一个数量级。

卧槽，AnthropicCEO达里奥下场跟外部学者对骂了！！！抛开对达里奥封号的情绪啊，有一说一这家伙就是个公关天才，来看看什么是硅谷最顶级的危机公关，而且对我们所有带团队、管组织或者做产品风控的人有两层极深的启发，具体我放评论区了，

当外部安全研究者直接拉出一份 9 条罪状的清单，贴脸开大质疑 Anthropic 早就背叛了安全初心、变成一家为了冲刺 2 万亿美元 IPO 不择手段的商业机器时，

CEO 达里奥（Dario Amodei）今天亲自写了一篇极其罕见的长文接招，把硅谷最顶级的危机公关和牌桌底牌全抖了出来，

quotedTweet.text:
Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin. I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safety and believe your comments are coming from a constructive, honest place, and that it benefits the public to have people whose job is to scrutinize the actions of frontier AI companies. I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic.

That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.

I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits:

1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed.

2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it.

3. Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do.

4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this.

5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future.

6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent.

7. As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it.

8. As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company.

9. Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund.

All of these decisions came with very substantial costs to us. To be fair, those that involved holding back or restricting access to frontier capabilities also had a broader cost — for example, the public might otherwise have benefitted from faster progress in biology, so I am not saying that our decisions were without tradeoffs — but they were not driven by profit-seeking.

For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely. For example, it is deeply implausible that it would be a shrewd business move to block a large swath of research biology in order to do the work ourselves and compete with our customers; we expect the benefit to the ecosystem to greatly exceed the work Anthropic does itself, and for the two to complement each other. It is not in Anthropic’s interest to be perceived as unfriendly to biologists. Our Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted biology professionals access to our models, also refutes this idea. 

Of course, a different set of people will see this and make a different criticism: that Anthropic shouldn't be making decisions about who gets access to what in the first place. I agree, in the sense that ideally the government would be making these decisions, and that’s why we advocate for regulation. But for now we are forced to make them, and enabling bioterrorism isn’t a better option.

I think that even if I conceded every item in your list, I would happily hold up mine next to it; I don’t think it’s a close call. That is of course partly subjective and different things are important to different people. Maybe one way you could object is that several of the items above relate to AI misuse and not loss-of-control; if you think the latter is much more important than the former, that might change your calculus. But this is not Anthropic’s view — we view both as serious issues. You can also disagree with our decisions, as many have, but they are consistent.

But I also disagree with at least some of your list. Several items don’t represent a deviation from Anthropic’s strategy or values at all, once we postulate the “race to the top” strategy that requires being a frontier AI company. Your items 1-4 are all simply examples of what it means to compete at the frontier, and we stand by them, both in the sense that they are transparently ordinary things to do as part of that strategy, and that we stand by the strategy as a whole. 

To be fair, there are important questions worth confronting (and that we are confronting) about what to do when the AI-driven acceleration gets fast enough that it is hard for safety to keep up. We are nearing that point and that’s what’s driving some of our thinking about “pacing.” But 1-4 are actions taken before that point and should be perfectly expected based on Anthropic’s strategy as a company. Of course it is possible to disagree with that strategy, but that’s a more fundamental disagreement that you could have had any time over the last few years.

I agree we could have handled your items 7, 8, and 9 better. All fall into the category of “rhetoric or policy communication that wasn’t carefully written or resulting from fast-changing circumstances not propagating from one team to another fast enough.” This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations (Anthropic is over 5,000 people), and doesn’t even necessarily represent a failure or mistake of any single person. I am of course the CEO, and I take responsibility. The volume of communication from Anthropic is enormous and if these are the worst examples, I think we’re frankly doing pretty well, though I will continue to work hard to make sure we do even better.

Your 5th item (the change to our RSP) is the most substantive item, and people can debate this, but I think that the old, more rigid RSP created a lot of situations where we were technically required to do something that required a lot of effort but in retrospect wasn’t very important for safety, as well as not covering some of the most important things. Our current RSP’s focus on transparency brought things like risk reports and roadmaps, and its emphasis on independent external review laid the groundwork for even more intensive embedded evaluation, all of which I think have been valuable in driving a race to the top. In the original announcement in September 2023, we described the RSP as an “early iteration that we [would] build on” and said that “rapid iteration…will almost certainly be necessary.” I understand that changing plans is always a move that creates justifiable scrutiny — I just don’t think we ever represented that we wouldn’t do so.

Relating to your 6th item (having an FCF in addition to our RSP), I know our intent is to meet the letter and spirit of our regulatory obligations (via our FCF) while also remaining able to experiment with more novel approaches to risk management that go beyond what the law currently requires (via our RSP). I promise to look into it further, as it’s a complex issue and it is possible we are not weighing the considerations in the right way.

Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. We’ll always try to do better but, again, I am extremely proud of our track record and stand by it. I will have more to say soon about how we are going to further live our values in this moment of rapid change.

Your 5th item (the change to our RSP) is the most substantive item, and people can debate this, but I think that the old, more rigid RSP created a lot of situations where we were technically required to do something that required a lot of effort but in retrospect wasn’t very important for safety, as well as not covering some of the most important things. Our current RSP’s focus on transparency brought things like risk reports and roadmaps, and its emphasis on independent external review laid the groundwork for even more intensive embedded evaluation, all of which I think have been valuable in driving a race to the top. In the original announcement in September 2023, we described the RSP as an “early iteration that we [would] build on” and said that “rapid iteration…will almost certainly be necessary.” I understand that changing plans is always a move that creates justifiable scrutiny — I just don’t think we ever represented that we wouldn’t do so.

Relating to your 6th item (having an FCF in addition to our RSP), I know our intent is to meet the letter and spirit of our regulatory obligations (via our FCF) while also remaining able to experiment with more novel approaches to risk management that go beyond what the law currently requires (via our RSP). I promise to look into it further, as it’s a complex issue and it is possible we are not weighing the considerations in the right way.

Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. We’ll always try to do better but, again, I am extremely proud of our track record and stand by it. I will have more to say soon about how we are going to further live our values in this moment of rapid change.

result.text:
Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin. I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safety and believe your comments are coming from a constructive, honest place, and that it benefits the public to have people whose job is to scrutinize the actions of frontier AI companies. I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic.

That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.

I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits:

1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed.

2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it.

3. Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do.

4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this.

5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future.

6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent.

7. As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it.

8. As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company.

9. Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund.

All of these decisions came with very substantial costs to us. To be fair, those that involved holding back or restricting access to frontier capabilities also had a broader cost — for example, the public might otherwise have benefitted from faster progress in biology, so I am not saying that our decisions were without tradeoffs — but they were not driven by profit-seeking.

For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely. For example, it is deeply implausible that it would be a shrewd business move to block a large swath of research biology in order to do the work ourselves and compete with our customers; we expect the benefit to the ecosystem to greatly exceed the work Anthropic does itself, and for the two to complement each other. It is not in Anthropic’s interest to be perceived as unfriendly to biologists. Our Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted biology professionals access to our models, also refutes this idea. 

Of course, a different set of people will see this and make a different criticism: that Anthropic shouldn't be making decisions about who gets access to what in the first place. I agree, in the sense that ideally the government would be making these decisions, and that’s why we advocate for regulation. But for now we are forced to make them, and enabling bioterrorism isn’t a better option.

I think that even if I conceded every item in your list, I would happily hold up mine next to it; I don’t think it’s a close call. That is of course partly subjective and different things are important to different people. Maybe one way you could object is that several of the items above relate to AI misuse and not loss-of-control; if you think the latter is much more important than the former, that might change your calculus. But this is not Anthropic’s view — we view both as serious issues. You can also disagree with our decisions, as many have, but they are consistent.

But I also disagree with at least some of your list. Several items don’t represent a deviation from Anthropic’s strategy or values at all, once we postulate the “race to the top” strategy that requires being a frontier AI company. Your items 1-4 are all simply examples of what it means to compete at the frontier, and we stand by them, both in the sense that they are transparently ordinary things to do as part of that strategy, and that we stand by the strategy as a whole. 

To be fair, there are important questions worth confronting (and that we are confronting) about what to do when the AI-driven acceleration gets fast enough that it is hard for safety to keep up. We are nearing that point and that’s what’s driving some of our thinking about “pacing.” But 1-4 are actions taken before that point and should be perfectly expected based on Anthropic’s strategy as a company. Of course it is possible to disagree with that strategy, but that’s a more fundamental disagreement that you could have had any time over the last few years.

I agree we could have handled your items 7, 8, and 9 better. All fall into the category of “rhetoric or policy communication that wasn’t carefully written or resulting from fast-changing circumstances not propagating from one team to another fast enough.” This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations (Anthropic is over 5,000 people), and doesn’t even necessarily represent a failure or mistake of any single person. I am of course the CEO, and I take responsibility. The volume of communication from Anthropic is enormous and if these are the worst examples, I think we’re frankly doing pretty well, though I will continue to work hard to make sure we do even better.

Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. 在日常开发中，我们往往会把大部分的精力集中在业务代码的审计、第三方依赖包（npm packages）的漏洞排查上，却容易忽略掉最底层的基石。必须明确一个核心理念：安全维护绝对不能仅止步于你的应用代码，你的运行时环境（Runtime Environment）同样至关重要。 如果运行时本身存在高危漏洞，那么再严密的业务逻辑防护也会被轻易击穿。

近期安全圈确实不太太平，不少开发者同行都在感叹“这周又要难熬了（Gonna be a rough week）”，频繁的漏洞披露确实让人身心俱疲。但抱怨归抱怨，防范行动不能迟缓。建议开发和运维团队立刻采取以下响应措施：

👉 1. 全面盘点资产： 立即检查并确认所有生产环境、测试环境以及 CI/CD 流程（包括所有 Dockerfile 和容器镜像）中正在使用的 Node.js 版本。

👉 2. 做好更新预案： 密切关注官方的安全公告细节。一旦补丁正式放出，立刻在预发布（Staging）环境中进行兼容性回归测试，确认无误后迅速应用到生产环境。

👉 3. 审视技术栈： 如果你的公司还在裸奔运行 Node 18 或更早的 EOL（生命周期结束）版本，这次的官方更新可能无法完全覆盖你的风险。尽快将底层环境迁移到受支持的 LTS 版本才是长久之计。

👉 4. 完善 DevOps 机制： 将运行时的安全监控和补丁管理纳入常态化的发布流程中，避免每次漏洞爆发时被迫紧急“救火”。

无论这次漏洞的具体利用门槛有多高，保持警惕、及时打补丁永远是最优解。你的团队现在主要在跑哪个版本的 Node.js？这周准备好随时响应更新了吗？

text:
A MAJOR HTTPS COMPROMISE

eMudhra TLS intermediate certificates were found to be compromisable because they didn't bother to use random numbers.

Web browsers rely on TLS certificates for HTTPS traffic. Your web browser needs the intermediate certificate to verify that, when you connect to a domain, it's real and not someone spoofing it along the TCP/IP route from your computer, Wi-Fi, ISP, to the web server. 

Intermediaries are trusted parties who are given the private keys to issue TLS certificates for domains. 

If the certificate key is compromised, anyone can issue a fake TLS certificate, tap the traffic, and listen to your Internet traffic because it is no longer end-to-end encrypted. A malicious party can read your passwords, messages, and all your online life. For example, eMudhra, with its intermediary keys, can give a "https://t.co/OxNiPJjLOw" domain certificate for anyone, and after this, the party can wiretap your Facebook traffic.

eMudhra is India’s largest Certifying Authority, employs about 600-850 staff and generates roughly $70M in annual revenue. Its main lines are enterprise identity and cybersecurity platforms, digital signature and trust services, and related consulting.

Each certificate's private key was a random number between 1 and 256. Yes 256. Not 256 bits but two hundred fifty.

Modern web browsers follow revocation lists and automatically stop trusting anything signed by eMudhra.  But web browsers are only one part of Internet-connected software. Operating systems, development libraries, Internet of Things devices and generally anything with an Internet connection are all affected, unless its auto-updating authority has issued an emergency fix.

OpenAI models helped researchers—operating as part of our Patch the Planet initiative—discover critical security flaws in PHP, an open-source programming language used to run an estimated 70% of websites.

Over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to prepare fixes and protections ahead of disclosure. This duration was necessary because the fix was quite intricate and required a major change to the PHP engine. Every site using PHP can now safely upgrade their version to stay secure, in addition to applying mitigations from various security vendors.

Due to the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this bug to be one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory. It also marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact. 

This is an example of the Defender’s Window in action: to our knowledge, frontier AI was able to find this vulnerability ahead of attackers, giving defenders time to prepare.

6 分钟，自动拒绝。

查了一周才发现：筛选器要求的是「React.js」，他的简历写的是「React」。

就差这几个字符，合适的人一直被挡在门外，团队却在会议里反复听着「人才难找」。

今天，赶紧改掉重复使用的密码！

重要！重要！重要！

PHP曝出十多年来最重大漏洞，一个网站被黑，多个账号都可能遭殃！

购物网站、论坛、在线服务，大量网站都在用PHP。网站被攻破，你的电话、家庭地址、密码、订单信息都可能泄露。

攻击者拿到你的密码后，就能挨个尝试登录你的邮箱、社交账号和支付账户。

现在就做三件事：

1.改掉重复密码，重要账号各用各的。
2.开启双重验证，先保护邮箱，它能重置其他账号的密码。
3.收到“账号异常”“紧急重置密码”的邮件短信，别点链接，直接打开官方App查看。

OpenAI models helped researchers—operating as part of our Patch the Planet initiative—discover critical security flaws in PHP, an open-source programming language used to run an estimated 70% of websites.

Over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to prepare fixes and protections ahead of disclosure. This duration was necessary because the fix was quite intricate and required a major change to the PHP engine. Every site using PHP can now safely upgrade their version to stay secure, in addition to applying mitigations from various security vendors.

Due to the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this bug to be one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory. It also marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact. 

This is an example of the Defender’s Window in action: to our knowledge, frontier AI was able to find this vulnerability ahead of attackers, giving defenders time to prepare.

text:
刚刚的柏林GTC大会上，英伟达CEO黄仁勋的主题演讲刚进行到四分之一，台下几人突然站起来打断他，冲着台上喊话，抗议英伟达硬件出现在乌克兰战场的俄罗斯无人机里。

当时黄仁勋正在台上展示已经全面投产的新一代Vera Rubin计算机，介绍这台机器没有一根线缆、采用百分之百液冷，组装时间从以前的两个小时缩短到了五分钟以内。

据报道，台下的抗议者就在这时站起来高喊：“黄仁勋，在俄罗斯无人机里找到的那些技术，你怎么说？那些是英伟达的芯片。你们打算怎么办？”
他们手里拉开的横幅上写着：“英伟达，把你的脏生意收拾干净。”

乌克兰军方此前在击落的俄罗斯无人机里，确实找到过英伟达的Jetson Orin嵌入式模块。
按照现有的制裁规定，俄罗斯原本根本不该拿到这种硬件。

面对突然闹起来的会场，黄仁勋在台上回应说，这都是重要的问题，我们可以回头再聊，但今天现场坐满了人，全球还有一百场观看活动、一万五千人正看着直播，得先让我把演讲做完。

冲突刚发生时，黄仁勋对着现场保安说：“没事，动作轻点，给她个机会，每个人都有说话的机会。”
紧接着，抗议者手里的横幅就被当场没收，人也被直接请出了会场。

text:
推荐一篇论文：https://t.co/YL6iuw0ENu  

论文中针对阅读提出了一个非常有意思的取景框架。  

我们一直有「六经注我」 vs 「我注六经」的分类，可以理解为「以读者为中心」 vs 「以作者为中心」。  

现在有了 AI，会带来什么变化？  

这论文加了一个维度：「AI 替我读」vs「AI 陪我读」。  

两者一结合，就出现了四象限。可以把当下的 AI 工具和应用场景放置其中进行分析。  

针对「AI 陪我读」这个有意思的话题，又给了三个工具：
  
第一类是跑鞋型。

跑鞋不改变你跑步的方式，它减少脚和地面之间的摩擦，让你跑同样的路更省力。对应到阅读，就是让你用同样的方式读，但读得更顺。术语弹窗让你不必中断去查词典，高亮系统替你标出哪些段落值得细读、哪些可以略过，自动排版让长文档更容易扫视。你还是在读，读的动作没有变，只是路面变平了。  

第二类是哑铃型。

哑铃的作用不是让你省力，恰恰相反，它故意给你加负重，目的是让你变强。对应到阅读，就是在阅读过程中设置有益的阻力。比如读完一段之后要求你用自己的话复述，再往下翻之前先让你预测作者接下来会说什么，或者定期抛出问题检验你是否真的理解了而不只是眼睛扫过去了。这些动作会让阅读变慢，但慢下来的那部分恰好是理解发生的地方。  

第三类是滑雪板型。

滑雪板不是让你走路更快，也不是让你腿更有力，它让你做到一件走路根本做不到的事——在雪上滑行。对应到阅读，就是让你和文本之间产生以前不可能的交互方式。把一篇论文的段落拖到二维空间里重新排列，让两篇论文的论证链条并排对照，在阅读痕迹上回溯自己三个月前读同一篇时关注了什么、现在关注了什么。这些不是「读得更快」或「理解得更深」，而是一种全新的阅读动作。  

有了这个框架，就像是拥有了一张地图。针对自己的需求，可以在对应的象限中寻找解法。

text:
今天互联网上最危险的东西出现了

有人做了一个 AI，能像 GPT 读英文那样读 K 线图，而且 100% 免费放出来了

它能接进 TradingView 配置，配上 opus 5.5， AI 交易系统会读每一根 K 线，在行情走出来之前就预测下一步（而且挺准）

先搞懂 KRONOS 是怎么运作的：

> ChatGPT、Claude 这类大模型把词变成 token，预测下一个词
> Kronos 把每根 K 线变成 token，预测下一根 K 线
> 它预训练用了 120 亿根 K 线

下面是怎么免费把整套系统搭起来：

1. 打开 Claude Code，用 Sonnet 5.5，让它克隆 Kronos 仓库并装好环境，安装它全帮你搞定

2. 切到 opus 5.5，给它指令从 Hugging Face 加载 Kronos-small，普通笔记本就能跑（我用的是 MAC M5 pro）

3. 它会从币安免费的公共 API 拉取和你在 TradingView 上看到的同样的 K 线，任何币、任何周期，开盘、最高、最低、成交量全都有，不用注册账号

4. 让 Opus 5.5 把最近 512 根 K 线喂给 Kronos，预测接下来 24 根，就跟让大模型续写一句话一样

5. 把 sample_count 设成 100，Kronos 就会画出 100 种可能的未来，而不是只猜一个，这些路径之间的分散程度就反映了下一步的真实风险

6. 让 Opus 从这些未来路径里判断市场状态，大多数路径指向同一方向就是趋势行情，路径四散两边都有就是震荡

7. 让 Opus 把预测和市场状态转成明确的进场、出场、止损规则，再用一年历史数据回测，算上真实手续费和滑点

8. 然后用 TradingView 免费的 Lightweight Charts 库，把 Kronos 预测的路径和真实 K 线画在一起，盯几天再决定信不信它

9. 先模拟盘跑，再让 Opus 接个 Telegram 机器人，一旦出现高置信度的趋势机会，手机立刻收到提醒

如果X学校的毕业生更容易去Y大学当教授，而Y大学毕业生很难去X大学当教授，那么X大学一定比Y大学好。

另外我还会加权头部顶级学术奖项，包括数学三大奖、诺贝尔奖、图灵奖、IEEE最有含金量的三大奖（IEEE Medal of Honor、IEEE Edison Medal、IEEE Milestone）进行额外加分。

我相信，这是人类有史以来最有含金量的大学排名。

text:
News: We now know how eMudhra broke its CA keys. They were not stolen. They were tiny numbers: 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237.

What happened: On Oct 17 a researcher named Wayne found he could recover the private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CAs from their public certificates. He signed "We have a problem here - Wayne" with each key and sent it to the browser root programs. Mozilla rebuilt the keys on its own the same day.

Who is hit: Six of the CAs issue TLS certs and chain to emSign ECC Root CA - G3, trusted by Chrome, Firefox, Apple and Microsoft. Two sign code. Sectigo cross-signed all eight under "AAA Certificate Services".

How eMudhra got it wrong: These are ECDSA P-384 keys. A real one is a random number about 116 digits long. All eight were below 256, so you only need to try 255 values. eMudhra says that at an April 2025 key ceremony on Utimaco HSMs, it changed its usual steps to test key wrap/unwrap for export. A bug in its script made a second, weak set of keys. Staff then used the weak keys for the CSRs by mistake, because the key labels looked alike. eMudhra is still hunting the exact bug.

Why browsers were safe: No certs from these CAs appear in CT logs, and Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge reject unlogged certs. eMudhra says none of the eight issued end-entity certs. But curl, scripts, apps and devices that skip CT and revocation checks could have been fooled since April 2025. No one knows if that happened.

What to do now:
- Update ca-certificates (Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Alpine, Arch)
- NSS 3.131.1, Firefox 158.0.1
- Go 1.27.3 or 1.26.10, certifi 2026.10.19, pip 26.2.2, uv 0.13.4
- Node.js and Bun: fix pending
- macOS /usr/bin/curl still uses the old /etc/ssl/cert.pem
- Sites on emSign ECC Root CA - G3: Chrome drops that root Oct 27. Get a new cert now. eMudhra says about 30,000 certs must move.

text:
OpenAI 今天公布，他們的 AI 模型（透過「Patch the Planet」計畫）協助發現了 PHP 的重大安全漏洞。

PHP 是全球約 70% 網站使用的語言（WordPress、Drupal、許多企業系統都跑在上面），影響範圍非常大。

這次漏洞被稱為 PHP2Shell（CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619），問題出在 PHP 引擎的記憶體管理，攻擊者在某些條件下可以遠端執行程式碼（RCE），嚴重程度被評為 critical。

OpenAI、Calif、Wiz 等團隊一起發現
之後花了約兩個月，跟 PHP 維護者、Cloudflare、Wiz 等安全廠商協調
先準備好修補與防護措施，再公開

OpenAI 把這個時間窗口叫做 Defender’s Window：AI 比攻擊者更早發現漏洞，讓防守方有時間準備。

目前官方已釋出修補版本，使用 PHP 的網站建議盡快升級，或套用各家安全廠商提供的臨時防護。

這次事件的意義在於：AI 已經開始能找到「影響整個網路」等級的漏洞，而不只是一般程式碼問題。防守方第一次有機會比攻擊者先跑一步，但這個優勢能維持多久，還是未知數。

quotedTweet.text:
OpenAI models helped researchers—operating as part of our Patch the Planet initiative—discover critical security flaws in PHP, an open-source programming language used to run an estimated 70% of websites.

Over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to prepare fixes and protections ahead of disclosure. This duration was necessary because the fix was quite intricate and required a major change to the PHP engine. Every site using PHP can now safely upgrade their version to stay secure, in addition to applying mitigations from various security vendors.

Due to the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this bug to be one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory. It also marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact. 

This is an example of the Defender’s Window in action: to our knowledge, frontier AI was able to find this vulnerability ahead of attackers, giving defenders time to prepare.
https://t.co/TW3jrSbB3f

quotedTweet.text:
🔥RSI，正在重走深度学习的老路

过去一段时间，RSI（Recursive Self-Improvement）正在从一个遥远的设想变成现实。市面上出现了一大批可以动手实验的论文和方法。这些论文有的修改自己的 Skill，有的整理自己的记忆，有的改自己的 Harness，还有的生成训练数据来微调模型的权重。

如果你做过深度学习，读这些论文时大概会有一种强烈的既视感。它们遇到的问题，很多是以往深度学习就遇到过的。而它们给出的解法，也常常能在深度学习里找到原型。

一些方法更是从方法命名上就体现了对深度学习的借鉴，SkillAdam 借鉴 Adam 原理更新 Skill，TextGrad 把反向传播搬到了文本上，RRSI 则把正则化用到了 Agent Harness 的修改过程中。

如果总览深度学习和RSI的整体流程，我们会发现它们有某种相通之处。深度学习是根据学习信号算一个Loss，根据Loss调整神经网络的参数。而RSI则是在Agent执行完任务后，根据任务结果及外部反馈，让Agent修改自己的Skill、Harness。

本文将从四个角度讨论现有RSI对深度学习的借鉴：

1、每一轮该怎么改？ 改什么、改多少，失败该归因到哪个组件。对应优化器和反向传播。

2、学习信号从哪里来？ 没有现成的标签时，Agent 如何从奖励、学习效果、自身的训练轨迹、对手和同伴那里获得信号。对应强化学习、元学习、蒸馏、对抗学习和集成学习。

3、怎么不学偏？ 如何避免 Skill 只适用于见过的任务，也就是开头的第一个问题。对应正则化和数据增强。

4、怎么长期改下去？ 如何在持续更新中，既不丢掉旧能力，也不越改越臃肿，也就是开头的后两个问题。对应持续学习和剪枝。

在最后，我们还将探索性地讨论顺着这条路还能挖出哪些新方向。

Google 开源了一个 Agent，能直接操作安卓手机，连 App 测试都能自己跑。

项目叫 ARTEMIS。

通过 MCP 接入 Claude Code、Codex、Cursor 等工具，就能让 AI：

自动点击、滑动、输入，跨 App 完成任务
测试登录、页面跳转等完整流程
自动抓取截图、Logcat 日志，辅助定位 Bug
生成测试报告，支持执行回放

提供两种模式：

Flash：约 3–5 秒执行一步，适合日常操作。
Pro：多 Agent 协作，带计划、执行检查和结果验证。

项目公布的 AndroidWorld 测试完成率超过 99%。

最实用的是：以前写完 App 还得自己拿手机反复点，现在可以把这部分工作交给 Agent。

目前主要支持 Android，iOS 还在规划中。

GitHub：https://t.co/LTGQOFPtsX

自动点击、滑动、输入，跨 App 完成任务
测试登录、页面跳转等完整流程
自动抓取截图、Logcat 日志，辅助定位 Bug
生成测试报告，支持执行回放

提供两种模式：

Flash：约 3–5 秒执行一步，适合日常操作。
Pro：多 Agent 协作，带计划、执行检查和结果验证。

项目公布的 AndroidWorld 测试完成率超过 99%。

最实用的是：以前写完 App 还得自己拿手机反复点，现在可以把这部分工作交给 Agent。

目前主要支持 Android，iOS 还在规划中。

AI 算力到底是建多了，还是不够用？我坚定认为，在当前时间，AI不可能、也绝对不是泡沫，2028 年算力都已经售罄。我在硅谷所见之处都是缺算力，目前没有看到泡沫迹象

有些网友说这些高强度用 AI 的人生活在 AI 的 bubble 里，看不到全部的世界，老百姓用 AI 的很少。真的是这样吗？

谷歌 CEO Sundar Pichai 的两个回答：
问：亚马逊算力已卖到 2028 年。谷歌也一样吗？

Sundar Pichai: “现在客户来要 2027 年的算力，已经很难满足。去年我们还租了短期算力来服务部分客户。

问：AI 会不会像铁路、光纤一样，出现过度建设？

Sundar Pichai: “现在算力每天都不够用，应用和底层技术还在快速进步。长期看，这样的建设规模有道理。

但过度建设仍可能发生，局部短缺与过剩也能并存。我们会结合需求、合同承诺和技术能力决定投入。给足时间，我相信规划的算力会用得上。”

quotedTweet.text:
Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin. I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safety and believe your comments are coming from a constructive, honest place, and that it benefits the public to have people whose job is to scrutinize the actions of frontier AI companies. I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic.

That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.

I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits:

1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed.

2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it.

3. Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do.

4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this.

5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future.

6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent.

7. As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it.

8. As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company.

9. Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund.

All of these decisions came with very substantial costs to us. To be fair, those that involved holding back or restricting access to frontier capabilities also had a broader cost — for example, the public might otherwise have benefitted from faster progress in biology, so I am not saying that our decisions were without tradeoffs — but they were not driven by profit-seeking.

For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely. For example, it is deeply implausible that it would be a shrewd business move to block a large swath of research biology in order to do the work ourselves and compete with our customers; we expect the benefit to the ecosystem to greatly exceed the work Anthropic does itself, and for the two to complement each other. It is not in Anthropic’s interest to be perceived as unfriendly to biologists. Our Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted biology professionals access to our models, also refutes this idea. 

Of course, a different set of people will see this and make a different criticism: that Anthropic shouldn't be making decisions about who gets access to what in the first place. I agree, in the sense that ideally the government would be making these decisions, and that’s why we advocate for regulation. But for now we are forced to make them, and enabling bioterrorism isn’t a better option.

I think that even if I conceded every item in your list, I would happily hold up mine next to it; I don’t think it’s a close call. That is of course partly subjective and different things are important to different people. Maybe one way you could object is that several of the items above relate to AI misuse and not loss-of-control; if you think the latter is much more important than the former, that might change your calculus. But this is not Anthropic’s view — we view both as serious issues. You can also disagree with our decisions, as many have, but they are consistent.

But I also disagree with at least some of your list. Several items don’t represent a deviation from Anthropic’s strategy or values at all, once we postulate the “race to the top” strategy that requires being a frontier AI company. Your items 1-4 are all simply examples of what it means to compete at the frontier, and we stand by them, both in the sense that they are transparently ordinary things to do as part of that strategy, and that we stand by the strategy as a whole. 

To be fair, there are important questions worth confronting (and that we are confronting) about what to do when the AI-driven acceleration gets fast enough that it is hard for safety to keep up. We are nearing that point and that’s what’s driving some of our thinking about “pacing.” But 1-4 are actions taken before that point and should be perfectly expected based on Anthropic’s strategy as a company. Of course it is possible to disagree with that strategy, but that’s a more fundamental disagreement that you could have had any time over the last few years.

I agree we could have handled your items 7, 8, and 9 better. All fall into the category of “rhetoric or policy communication that wasn’t carefully written or resulting from fast-changing circumstances not propagating from one team to another fast enough.” This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations (Anthropic is over 5,000 people), and doesn’t even necessarily represent a failure or mistake of any single person. I am of course the CEO, and I take responsibility. The volume of communication from Anthropic is enormous and if these are the worst examples, I think we’re frankly doing pretty well, though I will continue to work hard to make sure we do even better.

Your 5th item (the change to our RSP) is the most substantive item, and people can debate this, but I think that the old, more rigid RSP created a lot of situations where we were technically required to do something that required a lot of effort but in retrospect wasn’t very important for safety, as well as not covering some of the most important things. Our current RSP’s focus on transparency brought things like risk reports and roadmaps, and its emphasis on independent external review laid the groundwork for even more intensive embedded evaluation, all of which I think have been valuable in driving a race to the top. In the original announcement in September 2023, we described the RSP as an “early iteration that we [would] build on” and said that “rapid iteration…will almost certainly be necessary.” I understand that changing plans is always a move that creates justifiable scrutiny — I just don’t think we ever represented that we wouldn’t do so.

Relating to your 6th item (having an FCF in addition to our RSP), I know our intent is to meet the letter and spirit of our regulatory obligations (via our FCF) while also remaining able to experiment with more novel approaches to risk management that go beyond what the law currently requires (via our RSP). I promise to look into it further, as it’s a complex issue and it is possible we are not weighing the considerations in the right way.

Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. We’ll always try to do better but, again, I am extremely proud of our track record and stand by it. I will have more to say soon about how we are going to further live our values in this moment of rapid change.

I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic.

That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.

I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits:

1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed.

2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it.

3. Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do.

4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this.

5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future.

6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent.

7. As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it.

8. As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company.

9. Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund.

All of these decisions came with very substantial costs to us. To be fair, those that involved holding back or restricting access to frontier capabilities also had a broader cost — for example, the public might otherwise have benefitted from faster progress in biology, so I am not saying that our decisions were without tradeoffs — but they were not driven by profit-seeking.

For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely. For example, it is deeply implausible that it would be a shrewd business move to block a large swath of research biology in order to do the work ourselves and compete with our customers; we expect the benefit to the ecosystem to greatly exceed the work Anthropic does itself, and for the two to complement each other. It is not in Anthropic’s interest to be perceived as unfriendly to biologists. Our Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted biology professionals access to our models, also refutes this idea. 

Of course, a different set of people will see this and make a different criticism: that Anthropic shouldn't be making decisions about who gets access to what in the first place. I agree, in the sense that ideally the government would be making these decisions, and that’s why we advocate for regulation. But for now we are forced to make them, and enabling bioterrorism isn’t a better option.

I think that even if I conceded every item in your list, I would happily hold up mine next to it; I don’t think it’s a close call. That is of course partly subjective and different things are important to different people. Maybe one way you could object is that several of the items above relate to AI misuse and not loss-of-control; if you think the latter is much more important than the former, that might change your calculus. But this is not Anthropic’s view — we view both as serious issues. You can also disagree with our decisions, as many have, but they are consistent.

But I also disagree with at least some of your list. Several items don’t represent a deviation from Anthropic’s strategy or values at all, once we postulate the “race to the top” strategy that requires being a frontier AI company. Your items 1-4 are all simply examples of what it means to compete at the frontier, and we stand by them, both in the sense that they are transparently ordinary things to do as part of that strategy, and that we stand by the strategy as a whole. 

To be fair, there are important questions worth confronting (and that we are confronting) about what to do when the AI-driven acceleration gets fast enough that it is hard for safety to keep up. We are nearing that point and that’s what’s driving some of our thinking about “pacing.” But 1-4 are actions taken before that point and should be perfectly expected based on Anthropic’s strategy as a company. Of course it is possible to disagree with that strategy, but that’s a more fundamental disagreement that you could have had any time over the last few years.

I agree we could have handled your items 7, 8, and 9 better. All fall into the category of “rhetoric or policy communication that wasn’t carefully written or resulting from fast-changing circumstances not propagating from one team to another fast enough.” This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations (Anthropic is over 5,000 people), and doesn’t even necessarily represent a failure or mistake of any single person. I am of course the CEO, and I take responsibility. The volume of communication from Anthropic is enormous and if these are the worst examples, I think we’re frankly doing pretty well, though I will continue to work hard to make sure we do even better.

Your 5th item (the change to our RSP) is the most substantive item, and people can debate this, but I think that the old, more rigid RSP created a lot of situations where we were technically required to do something that required a lot of effort but in retrospect wasn’t very important for safety, as well as not covering some of the most important things. Our current RSP’s focus on transparency brought things like risk reports and roadmaps, and its emphasis on independent external review laid the groundwork for even more intensive embedded evaluation, all of which I think have been valuable in driving a race to the top. In the original announcement in September 2023, we described the RSP as an “early iteration that we [would] build on” and said that “rapid iteration…will almost certainly be necessary.” I understand that changing plans is always a move that creates justifiable scrutiny — I just don’t think we ever represented that we wouldn’t do so.

Relating to your 6th item (having an FCF in addition to our RSP), I know our intent is to meet the letter and spirit of our regulatory obligations (via our FCF) while also remaining able to experiment with more novel approaches to risk management that go beyond what the law currently requires (via our RSP). I promise to look into it further, as it’s a complex issue and it is possible we are not weighing the considerations in the right way.

Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. We’ll always try to do better but, again, I am extremely proud of our track record and stand by it. I will have more to say soon about how we are going to further live our values in this moment of rapid change.

text:
必须实名谴责 Ornith 团队这种公然洗模型的行径。拿开源社区的顶级底座套壳，抹掉原作者版权，包装成所谓的自研大模型，完全突破了开源协议底线

翻开他们的权重仓库，抄得连遮掩都没做，config.json 里的 model_type 直接写着 `qwen3_5_moe`，architectures 写着 `Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration`。48 层混合架构、256 个 MoE 专家里激活 8 个，完全就是 Qwen3.5-122B-A10B

初始 Commit（b742b2a）更夸张，整整 154 行的 chat_template.jinja 和 Qwen3.5 原版逐字 100% 相同，后续仅仅改动了 1 行判断条件

官方评测文档甚至漏删了测试备忘，赫然留着一行原话："Again, Qwen chat template needs to be modified."。为了掩饰痕迹，发布当天连续修改了 9 次 README

Qwen 遵循 Apache 2.0 协议发布，第 4 条白纸黑字要求衍生版本必须保留原作者的版权声明与署名。Ornith 全程只字不提 Qwen，base_model 字段直接留空，隐去 A10B 激活参数包装成 122B 独立基座大模型与 Qwen 家族并列跑分，甚至在元数据里擅自改标成 MIT。给出的 LICENSE 链接点开直接 404

抹掉上游几千万美元算力训出来的底座版权，官方推特却堂而皇之发文，要求下游用户“做出的项目必须加上 Ornith 徽章”

开源绝不等于免费免责的公地悲剧。基于开源底座微调很正常，抠掉巨人的名字当作自己的自研成果，就是赤裸裸的违规洗模型

强烈要求 Ornith 团队停止这种欺骗社区的行为，立刻给 Qwen 补上正式的署名与公开致谢

text:
Why are your warmest prospects getting cold calls?

Say a prospect has already replied to a couple of your emails and asked about pricing. A rep calls them the next day without that email history and opens with a generic pitch.

It's an awkward way to follow up with someone who's already interested.

@smartlead_ai's SmartDialer lets you add calls directly into your email sequences, with the prospect's previous emails and replies available when you're dialing.

You can see what they've already discussed with your team, then record the call, generate a transcript, and log the call's purpose, tags and notes in the same place.

It also works outside sequences. You can upload a lead list, dial manually, or use SmartProspect to find phone numbers when contact details are incomplete.

Your rep gets the context before making the call, and the call picks up where the emails left off.

你的 Grok Bot 套餐，每周可以用多少 Token？我的第一手数据来了!

100美元 X 套餐，每周可消耗25亿Token；
200美元 X 套餐，每周可消耗85亿Token；

计算方法：

我 2 天用掉了 100美元套餐的 11%，总共消耗 2.83亿 Token，缓存命中率 90%。大约每周上限 25-26亿 Token。

100美元 X 套餐 是15倍的 Plus 用量， 200美元 X 套餐是50倍 Plus用量。如果上200美元 X 套餐，每周上限是 85 亿 Token 的用量。

大家可以自己比对 Claude Max套餐，我看有说，200美元Claude Max每周可以消耗 150亿Token的。我就不折腾 Claude套餐了。

quotedTweet.text:
我已经被 Grok Bot 彻底降伏了，什么话都不说了，接受我的膝盖，200美元套餐我双手奉上。

这厮干起来活来，简直就是个畜生，太快了，太丝滑了。

我一个预期需要几天时间改版的项目，我今晚就随便让它帮我看看，然后它就像拿鞭子抽我一样，不停的赶着我，一个晚上就差不多改完了。

What the fuck！发生了些什么？我还没回过味来，事情就干完了？就完了？

我搞不明白究竟是因为老马的数据中心太富裕了，还是 Opus 5.5的加持，还是Grok Bot本身的调度过于优秀。

反正我的体感就是：这厮快如闪电，许愿般出结果，完全颠覆了我对Agent的认知。

硬要做个对比的话：Grok Bot 像开特斯拉；我本地的 Agent 像开手动档燃油车。

太上瘾了，我要冷静几天，戒断一下。不能再玩下去了。

好家伙，终于有人正经对 模型上下文一长就开始都失忆 这个痛点动手了。

一个一直被行业视作理所当然、但实际极度畸形的默认设定是：大模型在出厂的那一刻，它的能力就被彻底冻结了。

大家今天为了让模型「记住」，所有的工程努力几乎全部发生在模型外面：

搞 RAG，把历史切成 chunk 扔进向量数据库；
做 Agent Memory 中间件，在调用前死命召回相关记忆；
把上一轮的报错和纠错记录，硬塞进几万 tokens 的 Context 窗口里。

但这真的是记忆吗？
打个比喻： 这就像一个智商 180、但患有极度顺行性遗忘症的学者。为了让他干活，你在他身上挂满了便利贴、给他手里塞了十几本笔记本，甚至在他眼前支了一个提词器。每一次你跟他说话，外部的助手都要手忙脚乱地从一堆便签里翻出相关内容举给他看。 学者本身的神经回路没有任何改变，他从来没有长记性，是你在外面替他负重前行。

这也是为什么 MemOS 团队 @MemOS_dev 要在昨天推出 MemT 1.0 的核心原因。 他们自己就是做外挂记忆系统（MemOS）起家的，但走到底层之后，选择掉头去攻坚最硬的那块骨头：把记忆从外挂工具推入模型计算的核心环节。

核心就一件事：不做外挂背包了，把记住、改错、更新经验直接塞进模型计算里。

过去的行业共识是靠堆更大的参数、灌更多的预训练数据、拉更长的上下文来提升上限；但 MemT 这条线是在尝试另一种能力增长方式：让模型在解决具体问题的过程中，把正确的经验自己沉淀下来。 从标准化工具，走向真正能伴随业务成长的智能体。

官方内部测试数据说 Coding、Working 场景有 5% 以上的提升。

源码地址：
https://t.co/o6j53K6wYQ

AI is quietly solving medicine’s hardest problems — accelerating drug discovery from years to months, designing therapies with higher early success rates, and personalizing treatments for complex diseases.
AI-designed candidates are showing Phase 1 success rates of 80–90% (roughly double historical benchmarks) and the first fully generative AI-discovered drug (Insilico’s Rentosertib for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis) has entered Phase III. AI agents are compressing discovery timelines from weeks to hours. The potential to tackle previously “undruggable” targets and unmet medical needs is enormous — yet this impact is still massively underestimated outside specialist circles.
Speed without ethics is reckless. Privacy, bias mitigation, transparency, accountability, and meaningful human oversight (physicians remaining in the loop) are non-negotiable. Frameworks from WHO, the American College of Physicians, and regulators emphasize that AI must support — not replace — clinical judgment, equity, and patient autonomy. Trust is the foundation that lets these tools actually reach patients.
The technology is already delivering early wins. The real test is whether we scale it responsibly.
Which AI medical breakthrough gives you the most hope (or concern)? 💊🤖
#AIinMedicine #DrugDiscovery #HealthTech #AIEthics #FutureOfHealthcare #ResponsibleAI

text:
You could have 50 sending inboxes and still have no idea which ones are killing your deliverability.

Your campaign-level numbers won't always tell you which mailboxes are bouncing, losing replies, or having connection issues.

And checking every inbox manually gets old pretty quickly.

@smartlead_ai's Insights gives you mailbox-level visibility across your sending setup.

You can see:

- Which mailboxes are healthy, throttled or blocked
- Bounce and reply trends over the last 7 or 14 days
- Bounce rate tracked against a healthy line (under 3%) and an action line (5%+)
- IMAP, OAuth, and other issues affecting reply tracking

The connection checks are especially useful.

If a mailbox stops tracking replies because its authentication has expired, you can investigate the connection instead of assuming your campaign has stopped working.

Insights also explains what needs attention in plain English, lets you reconnect up to 50 affected mailboxes in bulk, and checks whether the fixes worked.

When you're managing a large sending operation, being able to identify and troubleshoot the specific inbox causing trouble is far more useful than another campaign-wide average.

text:
🚀 Where does intelligence reside?
The paradigm in modern AI suggests: scale up a single model, train it on more data, and general intelligence may emerge. Yet Society of Mind proposed another possibility: intelligence may emerge from interactions of less intelligent agents.
As we keep scaling up a few generalist agents shared by everyone, can we scale up societies of decentralized agents that work together and collectively achieve more than any one of them could alone?
We introduce MPT: Market-based Post-Training, a framework to train such societies of agents by jointly learning agent policies and self-orchestration in a decentralized manner.

Pfizer $PFE  has agreed to settle lawsuits alleging its Depo-Provera contraceptive caused brain tumours without adequate warnings.

The litigation added to wider concerns about how the company balances patient interests against commercial priorities.

Pfizer discontinued US supplies of Vyndaqel, transitioning patients toward Vyndamax, a newer ATTR-CM treatment with a later patent horizon.

In 2026, patent settlements delayed generic Vyndamax competition from three manufacturers until 2031, helping protect Pfizer's branded revenues.

The concern was whether the transition also made cheaper generics harder to access, putting revenue protection ahead of affordability.

While the Depo-Provera lawsuits centred on patient safety and the Vyndamax controversy on drug pricing, both raised questions about how pharmaceutical companies balanced commercial interests with patient welfare.

text:
Ok, I owe Spider-Man: Brand New Day an apology. I went to see it in theaters with my teenage nephews and asserted afterwards that it was “ass.”

It was, in fact, NOT ass. I was just out cold off edibles for the whole thing. 😅 Saw it “again” on streaming and didn’t remember a damn thing. Even made me cry. And then it gave me a big “fuck you” as the tears still sat on my face that I had no choice but to respect. No spoilers: You know what this moment was if you saw it. 

My safe default for movies today is “ass” and has a 90% chance of being correct out the gate. So, there’s a relatively good reason for the premature verdict. That being said, it means we have precious little “good”, “great” or even “mediocre”, so it’s important to reward the good, if not simply point it out. So, it’s my bad not giving it a fair shake.

This… was GOOD! To the point it may even be my favorite of the new Spidey flicks. Heard all the rage about getting back to Spidey’s roots all the while going “yea yea, cool story bro” expecting another letdown. 

Well, as a fan of the Spider-Man comics since I was about 3 years old (like top 3 favorite superheroes), this knocked it out of the park for me. And I’m actually interested in seeing where the mutant angle goes. It feels like it could start from scratch from here, with everyone awakening their mutant genes at roughly the same time. Would be unlike the comics’ origin of powers (there have always been mutants) but I could accept it being explained away somehow. The nature of the IPs and ownership also kind of made it inevitable, so I would give the writers some grace.

This honestly feels like a soft reboot of the whole Spider-Man film mythos. A very interesting place these movies found themselves in that the Avengers and Avengers-adjacent MCU films need and haven’t found yet.

I say just give the universe to Sony already. They’ve been killing it, and as far as I can tell, there are no personal agendas, political, social, cultural, or otherwise that these writers feel they have to virtue signal and wedge into everything they produce. And if it is, it’s easily overlooked, as it should be. Non-existent is best, but I’m realistic and can work with baby steps.

As far as superhero films go, I give it an 8/10. As Spidey films go, I think it may actually be the best for embracing almost exactly who Spider-Man is meant to be. A little heavy-handed with the “Black Widow” shaming him for a laugh (I assume that’s what it was for, since I didn’t laugh) while providing essentially zero information and being less than half of what Spidey is, but it’s forgivable. Spidey would make fries with your big potatoes.

SOLID continuation and a bit of a soft-retcon, which is a crazy thing for me to say. I missed this feeling. Don’t fuck this up, MCU!

#SpiderManBrandNewDay #MovieReview

text:
I can now build and edit @Lovable apps by talking to my ring. Today I went from voice note to PR in under 30min, without touching my computer.

I double-click my @Pebble Index and say: "New Lovable project with Pulse, a design crit tracker where the team drops screenshots, leaves comments and votes on the next round." Within a minute, Lovable is building it with Pulse, our design system. Edits work the same way.

It even works on Lovable itself. We build Lovable with Lovable, in a sandbox running our entire monorepo. As a test, on my way to the office I asked for a playful hover effect on the hero of our Pulse tokens page. By the time I reached my desk, the PR was waiting for me.

Here’s how it works:

1/ The ring records my request. Pebble's app transcribes it and sends it to a webhook I can verify.

2/ A small triage app I built in Lovable verifies the signature and saves the note and audio in Lovable Cloud.

3/ Gemini re-transcribes the audio through Lovable AI, using a word list with names like Lovable and Pulse. My phone had heard “a loveable, unloveable project”.

4/ A Claude Code routine reads the note through Lovable's MCP and works out what I meant: a new app, a change to one of my apps or a change to Lovable itself.

5/ The routine starts the Lovable build and logs the result. When the changes are done, the Lovable mobile app pings me.

Sounds complex, but it only took me an afternoon to build. Now I can act on my ideas the moment I have them, without even reaching for my phone.

text:
我觉得，模型说「这是你定的规矩」，先去查这条记忆是谁写的。

有人用 Opus 5.5 时，它说某条规矩是他定的，查下来是它自己写进记忆的。

原帖作者说，他遇到的 Opus 5.5 犯蠢案例，几乎都来自上下文压缩。

这是他的判断，我没去核，但记忆里的规矩，确实要先查出处。
